# Type-place unfolding stays in a ring generated by roots of unity

[Proof catalogue](../../PROOFS.en.md) · [Reading and review status](../../STATUS.md)

### Statement

Fix a type place $P$ in the true column chain, with rational prime norm $q$, local ring $A=\mathcal O_{E,P}$ and coefficient field $K$. Let
$$
R_q=\mathbb Z[\zeta\in K:\zeta^{q(q-1)}=1].
$$
At every layer assume the chart matrices preserve the scaled reference lattices in both directions, as required by `ChIdx.Ok` at a type place. The additive phase $\psi:q^{-D}A\to K^\times$ is a character equal to $1$ on $A$, with $D\ge1$.

For an ordinary step $i<m-2$, the unfolded function `XiAt` of the original rectangular matrix has values in $R_q$. It vanishes unless that matrix is integral and is invariant under adding $q$ times any integral matrix. The penultimate function `PsiAt` has the same three properties as a function of the original matrix, for every fixed appended column. The terminal function `locTop` also has these properties as a function of the full target matrix for any fixed source vector $y$ with $qy$ integral. The three properties constitute `FnModAt` in the standard frames. In particular all values are integral at every coefficient prime.

### Support and coefficients before unfolding

In the enlarged source and target spaces, take the adapted bases of the [type-local matrix test](the-type-local-test-transforms-by-its-flag-character.md). The reference lattice has ordinary vectors of exponent $0$ and extra vector number $l$ of exponent $l+1$, with exponents giving the powers of $q$ multiplying the basis vectors. In this basis the test requires every entry of the entire rectangular matrix to be integral. The source dimension is exactly the size of the leading square used in the test. Therefore being in its support implies that the matrix maps the reference lattice into the target reference lattice.

The type test is invariant under adding $q$ times a map between these reference lattices. In the adapted basis all entries change by multiples of $q$, which keep their integrality, all tested divisibility by $q$, and every reduction used in a phase or a determinant. Its residue additive character takes values of order dividing $q$ since the residue field has order $q$, and its residue multiplicative characters take values of order dividing $q-1$. The extension by zero and the inverse of a nonzero character value leave the result in $R_q$.

The chart changes $g,h$ replace the enlarged argument $Y$ by $h^{-1}Yg$. This preserves the lattice test in both directions and carries an allowed perturbation to another one, since the chart matrices preserve the reference lattices. Their determinants are local units. Thus in the normalized factor `omPhi` the valuation powers of the square root of $q$ are zero, and the determinant factors are the residue character values at the reductions of the determinants. Both are roots of unity of order dividing $q-1$. The normalized function of $Y$ therefore still has all three properties for the reference lattices.

### The free entries and the ordinary sum

At the ordinary step, the enlarged matrix $Y$ contains the original matrix as the block between ordinary coordinates. The other entries are either fixed at $0$ or $1$ or are free parameters, as defined by `IsFree` and `xx1`. Each free parameter lies in an extra source column. When the target is an ordinary row, the source extra exponent exceeds its target exponent by at least $1$. When the target is an extra row with its index below that of the source extra column, the same inequality holds for the two extra exponents. In the special final free column, its extra index equals the number of target extra coordinates, so this inequality holds against all target rows. These exhaust the free positions.

On a nonzero summand, the enlarged map is supported on the reference lattice. Since the original block has exponent $0$ in both source and target, that block is integral. Thus if the finite sum is nonzero, at least one of its summands is nonzero and the original matrix is integral.

Adding $q$ times an integral matrix to the original block leaves the normalized factor unchanged for every parameter choice. Changing any free parameter by an integral scalar has the same effect. Indeed in the adapted basis the change in a free position is its increment times $q$ to the positive difference of the source and target exponents, so is in $qA$.

The additive argument `chArg` is the sum of the entries from extra source column number $l+1$ to extra target row number $l$, treating a missing entry as zero. In each existing such entry the source exponent is exactly one greater than the target exponent. Thus on the support, $q\operatorname{chArg}(Y)$ is integral. The phase $\psi(-\operatorname{chArg}(Y))$ is then of order dividing $q$. The perturbations just described change the argument by an integral scalar, so the phase is unchanged as long as the normalized factor is nonzero. If that factor is zero, the entire summand remains zero. In particular each summand lies in $R_q$, the sum is periodic in the original matrix modulo $q$, and each free parameter is periodic modulo $A$.

The average over an enlarged free-parameter box at first appears to divide by a power of $q$. For one coordinate, the values are $r/q^{A_0}$ for $0\le r<q^{A_0+B}$. Write $r=r_0+q^{A_0}k$, with $0\le r_0<q^{A_0}$ and $0\le k<q^B$. The integrand depends only on $r_0$ by the integral period. Thus each value in the smaller box occurs with multiplicity $q^B$, cancelling the normalization $q^{-B}$ of this coordinate. Apply this to every free position. The average is then a finite sum of $R_q$ values. The [inverse relative volume](the-unipotent-volume-denominator-is-a-power-of-the-local-prime.md) is an integer in the type case, and hence its multiplication preserves $R_q$. This finishes the ordinary case.

### The last two steps

In the penultimate step the target has no extra coordinates and the source has one. The enlarged map sends $(v,t)$ to $Xv+ty$. In the scaled source basis the extra column is $qy$. Thus nonzero support implies integrality of the original block $X$. A change of $X$ by $q$ times an integral matrix leaves the appended column fixed and changes the enlarged map by $q$ times an integral map in the reference bases. The same finite character argument applies to the normalized factor, which is the whole penultimate function.

In the terminal step the projected matrix test forces the hyperplane part of a supported argument to be integral and depends only on its integral entries modulo $q$. The Fourier factor forces the last row $\ell$ to be integral. Then $\ell y\in q^{-1}A$ by the bound on $y$, and its phase is a root of unity of order dividing $q$. The full matrix is integral when both factors are nonzero. A change of the full matrix by $q$ times an integral one preserves the projected factor and changes the Fourier argument by an integral scalar, so preserves the whole product. Finally every generator of $R_q$ satisfies a monic integer polynomial, and sums and products of algebraic integers are integral. This means exactly that the resulting coefficients have valuation at most $1$ in the multiplicative convention at every coefficient prime.
